title: Correlated Insulating States in Twisted Double Bilayer Graphene Enhanced by Interfacial Effect on CrOCl
authors: Ning Ma, Zekang Zhou, Chiara Cocchi, Maurice Bal, Maarten van Delft, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Steffen Wiedmann, Jian-Hao Chen, Mitali Banerjee
abstract: Interaction between different two dimensional materials can give rise to many exotic physical phenomena which are rarely observed in intrinsic materials. Recently, several theoretical and experimental works have revealed that magnetic proximity effect between pristine graphene and magnetic substrates can lead to the emergence of quantum anomalous Hall states and quantum spin Hall states. However, interplay between correlated states in graphene-based systems and magnetic materials has seldom been studied. Here we perform the transport measurement at ultrahigh magnetic field of twisted double bilayer graphene (TDBG) on CrOCl (COC) substrate, which is an antiferromagnetic material. Instead of a magnetic-exchange effect on graphene, we observe an enhanced correlated insulating state at half-filling factor of TDBG as a result of the charge-transfer process between TDBG and COC. The temperature and magnetic field dependence of this enhanced state are further studied. Our results demonstrate the influence of charge-related effect at the interface, and shed a light on a new route for manipulating the correlated states in graphene-based moiré systems using interfacial engineering.
summary: This experiment explores correlated insulating states in TDBG interfaced with $	ext{CrOCl}$. By measuring transport properties under high magnetic fields, the authors conclude that charge-transfer effects at the interface are responsible for enhancing these correlated states. This demonstrates a powerful method of interfacial engineering to control exotic electronic phases in moiré graphene systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the emergence and nature of correlated insulating states in twisted double bilayer graphene (TDBG) when interfaced with an antiferromagnetic substrate ($	ext{CrOCl}$). The core question is whether the observed effects are due to magnetic proximity or charge-transfer interactions.
main_result: The enhanced correlated insulating state at half-filling is primarily attributed to a charge-transfer effect between TDBG and $	ext{CrOCl}$, rather than direct magnetic exchange. This interfacial engineering opens a new route for controlling correlated states in moiré systems.
method: Transport measurements were performed using ultrahigh magnetic fields and low temperatures, analyzing longitudinal/Hall resistance, Landau fan diagrams, and temperature dependence of the insulating state.
model_or_system: The physical system is Twisted Double Bilayer Graphene (TDBG) placed on a $	ext{CrOCl}$ substrate. The analysis focuses on correlated electron behavior in this moiré heterostructure under external magnetic fields.
key_observables: Enhanced resistance at half-filling, thermal activation gap ($\Delta$), and the effective g-factor derived from temperature dependence measurements.
important_parameters: Ultrahigh magnetic field (up to 20 T), low temperatures ($10 	ext{ mK}$), and the charge-transfer doping regime.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the observed enhancement stems from a charge-related reconstruction of the band structure due to interfacial coupling, distinguishing it from purely magnetic effects.
figures_summary: Figures show gate maps indicating the charge-transfer boundary, Landau fan diagrams comparing states with and without CT effect, and plots demonstrating how the insulating gap ($\Delta$) and g-factor change with temperature and applied magnetic field.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the experimental platform and observing the correlated state. It then systematically analyzes the dependence of this state on external fields (B) and temperature (T), using quantitative diagnostics like $\Delta$ and $g$-factors to confirm the role of charge transfer over magnetism.
why_interesting: The work provides direct experimental evidence of how interfacial chemistry (charge transfer) can be used as a tuning knob to manipulate strongly correlated electronic phases in 2D materials, which is highly relevant for designing novel quantum devices.
